item.title: Economic growth stalled again in August, StatCan says
item.description: Statistics Canada says the economy stalled for a second month in a row in August, and early estimates suggest growth declined in September.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canada’s economy stalled for a second month in a row in August and may be set for a decline in September, Statistics Canada said Friday. StatCan said real gross domestic product was essentially unchanged in August, falling short of economists’ calls and the agency’s own early expectations for a gain of 0.2 per cent. Wholesale trade fell 1.4 per cent in the month as most subsectors contracted. StatCan said motor vehicle and vehicle parts wholesalers faced their first decline in seven months amid lower vehicle imports and weaker manufacturing activity in the subsector. Work to prepare the 2026 census was also winding down in the month, driving widespread contractions in public administration. Strength in mining and quarrying was more than offset by a decline in oil and gas extraction, StatCan said. Oil sands extraction was the biggest drag on growth due to maintenance at some facilities in northern Alberta. Maintenance outages at nuclear power plants in Ontario and New Brunswick also dragged down the utilities industry in August. Retail trade was among the bright spots in the month, posting 1.2 per cent growth and more than making up for a decline in July. Manufacturing rose for the fifth time in seven months, and the transportation and warehousing industry and finance and insurance sector also saw gains in August. StatCan’s early estimates for September suggest real GDP declined 0.1 per cent, driven by losses in manufacturing and mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction. Despite flat growth in July and August and signs of a decline in September, StatCan’s flash estimates still see real GDP expanding 1.3 per cent on an annualized basis in the third quarter, a slowdown from 3.3 per cent growth in the second quarter. Because the economy was coming off such a robust month in June, it provided a strong starting point for the third quarter. As a result, despite weakened activity over the three-month period, it still produces positive annualized growth when compared to the second quarter’s average. StatCan will provide its official quarterly estimates for the third quarter next month when it reports the September GDP figures. BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in a note to clients Friday that some of the weakness last quarter might be overstated, particularly as it relates to census-related slowdowns. “Still, with the trade tiff still flaring, housing struggling, and recent employment figures concerning, it certainly appears that growth has run into some pretty serious headwinds of late,” he said. The latest economic data comes two days after the Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent, the first hike in more than three years. Officials at the central bank argued that rate hikes were warranted to get ahead of looming inflation risks. Governor Tiff Macklem pointed to signs of resilience in the Canadian economy over the spring in justifying the decision. The central bank also revised up its expectations for growth on Wednesday. Monetary policymakers are expecting growth in the third quarter ended up at two per cent on an annualized basis, up from 1.5 per cent in its July forecasts. Many economists weighing in Friday argued the Bank of Canada’s somewhat rosier projections are at risk after StatCan data suggested middling growth in the third quarter. BMO, which had been in line with the central bank’s call for two per cent growth, trimmed its outlook to 1.5 per cent after Friday’s surprise. Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC, said in a note that the data suggested the economy “was already struggling for momentum even before this week’s interest rate hike.” A slower-than-expected economy could help relieve inflationary pressures and reduce the need for additional rate hikes, he added. The weak GDP results support a pause from the Bank of Canada at its final rate decision of the year in December, Grantham said, though he noted there’s plenty of additional economic data to come before that meeting. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

item.title: Uranium miner Cameco reports $43M Q3 profit, revenue edges up from year ago
item.description: Cameco Corp. reported a third-quarter profit attributable to equity holders of $43 million as its revenue edged up compared with a year ago.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: SASKATOON — Cameco Corp. reported a third-quarter profit attributable to equity holders of $43 million as its revenue edged up compared with a year ago. The uranium miner says the profit amounted to 10 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30 compared with a break even result in the same quarter last year. Revenue totalled $619 million for the quarter, up from $615 million a year ago. On an adjusted basis, Cameco reported a loss of $2 million or zero cents per diluted share compared with an adjusted profit of $32 million or seven cents per diluted share a year earlier. Cameco says its results for the quarter and first nine months of the year were generally lower than in 2025, primarily due to lower equity earnings from its investment in Westinghouse, as well as lower sales volumes and higher average unit cost of sales. The company says those factors were partially offset by higher realized prices. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

item.title: U.S. futures fall as Amazon, Intel and Alphabet weigh on Wall Street
item.description: U.S. futures are falling Friday as technology companies such as Amazon, Intel and Alphabet all tumble lower, pressuring Wall Street.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A sell-off for tech stocks is barreling into Friday and forcing the U.S. market down again, with Amazon and Intel leading the way this time. The S&P 500 fell 1.3 per cent and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down 2.5 per cent, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, though the rest of the market was holding up better for a second straight day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell a more modest 0.3 per cent, or 173 points. Amazon was one of the heaviest weights on the market and dropped 4.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through US$42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent US$94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record after telling investors that it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring because of similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers. Intel tumbled 28.8 per cent and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell far short of analysts’ expectations. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure, which hurts demand for Intel’s CPUs. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward US$77,000 from more than US$86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than US$6 billion worth of crypto at Binance. Coinbase Global fell 12.7 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4 per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 11.6 per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Such losses overshadowed strength for the rest of Wall Street, where many stocks rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. The market is heading toward a second straight day where the majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rises but get overwhelmed by losses for larger, more influential Big Tech stocks. Mondelez International climbed 4.6 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth. Colgate-Palmolive rose 4.7 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Exxon Mobil rose 2.3 per cent, and Chevron added 1.6 per cent after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Starbucks had a more muted move following its own better-than-expected profit report and slipped 0.2 per cent. Its revenue for the quarter fell short of analysts’ expectations. Expectations are high broadly for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. U.S. Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that pushes upward on inflation and usually drives yields higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2 per cent to US$113.04. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper action in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.
